t: Alexander Dubček's Action Programme of April 1968 promised freedom of the press, speech and movement, a partial decentralisation of the economy and a federal Czechoslovakia, under the continued leadership of the Communist Party, in what he called "socialism with a human face".

The Soviet Union tried negotiations at Čierna nad Tisou and Bratislava, and then, on the night of 20–21 August 1968, troops from the Soviet Union, Bulgaria, Poland and Hungary occupied the country; Dubček called on his people not to resist, and the resistance that followed was largely nonviolent.

Under Gustáv Husák, normalisation reversed almost all of the reforms from 1969; the federalisation of the country was the only formal change to survive, and the memory of 1968 stayed contested for decades.
dyk: By August 1968 the censor-free journal Literární listy had a circulation of 300,000, making it the most published periodical in Europe.
ev: Marxist intellectuals organise the Liblice Conference on Franz Kafka, which marks the start of the cultural democratisation of Czechoslovakia
At the Writers' Congress in June, Ludvík Vaculík, Milan Kundera and Antonín Liehm deliver speeches against the regime's control of literature
Alexander Dubček replaces Antonín Novotný as First Secretary of the Communist Party on 5 January
Dubček launches the Action Programme of liberalisations in April, under the slogan of "socialism with a human face"
The talks at Čierna nad Tisou and the Bratislava Declaration end with a compromise that the Soviet leadership soon abandons
Warsaw Pact troops invade on the night of 20–21 August, and Dubček is arrested and taken to Moscow
Jan Palach sets himself on fire in Wenceslas Square on 16 January; Dubček is replaced by Gustáv Husák in April

f.where: The Czechoslovak Socialist Republic, above all Prague, Bratislava and Wenceslas Square; the talks were held at Čierna nad Tisou and Bratislava, and Dubček was taken to Moscow after the invasion.
f.period: Slow de-Stalinisation under Antonín Novotný (late 1950s and 1960s); Dubček became First Secretary on 5 January 1968; the Action Programme of April 1968; talks at Čierna nad Tisou (29 July to 1 August) and the Bratislava Declaration (3 August); invasion on the night of 20–21 August 1968; normalisation from April 1969.
f.figures: Alexander Dubček, First Secretary of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia; Ludvík Svoboda, who became President in March; the reformers Josef Smrkovský, Oldřich Černík and František Kriegel; the hardliners Vasil Biľak, Drahomír Kolder and Oldřich Švestka; Eduard Goldstücker, head of the Writers' Union; the economist Ota Šik; Leonid Brezhnev for the Soviet Union; Gustáv Husák, who replaced Dubček in 1969.
f.outcome: The Warsaw Pact invasion ended the reforms. Gustáv Husák reversed almost all of them in a period of normalisation, and only the federalisation of the country into Czech and Slovak republics survived. Czechoslovakia remained a Soviet satellite state until the Velvet Revolution of 1989.
